lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: describe how nervous and hormonal communication control responses and understand the differences between the two systems

primer.text: You already know that nerves carry fast electrical signals and that glands release chemicals into the blood. This note puts the two control systems side by side — nervous and hormonal — so you can name the messenger, the route, the speed and the duration of each, and pick the right system for any response an exam question describes.

modules.title: The nervous system: electrical impulses at speed
modules.opening: Two control systems share the job of responding to change: the nervous system and the hormonal (endocrine) system. The nervous side sends electrical impulses along neurones at speeds reaching about 100 metres per second, which is why a hand jerks back from a flame before you have thought about it. Speed is its defining feature.
keyPoints: Humans run two control systems side by side: nervous and hormonal (endocrine).
Electrical impulses race along neurones at speeds reaching 100 metres per second.
That speed makes nervous control ideal for instant responses such as the withdrawal reflex.
Receptors, the central nervous system's decision-making centres, and effectors are all coordinated by this system.

low.restatement: The nervous system uses fast electrical impulses along neurones, so responses happen almost instantly.
low.analogy: It is the body's lightning network — instant messages, instant reactions.
low.examPointer: Quote the speed figure (up to 100 m/s) when asked why nervous responses are rapid.

medium.restatement: Electrical signalling lets receptors, CNS decision centres and effectors act as one coordinated loop for functions needing immediacy.
medium.analogy: Compare it with a landline phone call — direct, wired and immediate, unlike a letter in the post.
medium.examPointer: Link speed to the reflex example: the flame-withdrawal case shows why some functions cannot wait for hormones.

modules.title: The endocrine system and the head-to-head comparison
sourceHeadings: A comparison of the nervous and endocrine systems table
modules.opening: The endocrine system works by chemistry. Endocrine glands secrete hormones into the blood, which carries them everywhere, and each hormone acts on its specific target organs to change their activity. Because transport relies on circulation, hormonal control is slower than nerves, but its effects last longer and spread wider.
keyPoints: The endocrine system sends information as chemical messengers called hormones.
Hormones travel in the blood plasma and so reach the whole body.
Each hormone acts on one or more named target organs and changes what they do.
Endocrine glands produce and secrete the hormones.
Hormonal control suits functions that do not need instant responses.

low.restatement: Glands release hormones into the bloodstream; each chemical signal acts on target organs, working more slowly but lasting longer than nerve impulses.
low.analogy: Hormones are letters delivered by the postal service — slower than a phone call, but read by every addressed office.
low.examPointer: For comparison questions anchor on the table: electrical vs chemical, neurones vs bloodstream, fast vs slower, local vs widespread, brief vs lasting.

medium.restatement: Because hormones circulate, one secretion can touch many organs at once and persist until breakdown, trading speed for breadth and duration.
medium.analogy: A radio broadcast reaches every receiver in range and keeps repeating, while a phone call reaches exactly one listener.
medium.examPointer: Duration wording matters: hormonal effects last until the hormone is broken down — quote that clause.

glossary.definition: A nerve cell that transmits electrical impulses; nerves are bundles of neurones.
The rapid automatic pull-away of a body part from danger, such as a hand leaving a flame.
A chemical messenger carried by the blood that changes the activity of specific target organs.
A group of cells that produces and secretes hormones into the bloodstream.
